planting.note: Sow in fall so seed cold-stratifies naturally over winter, into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun on dry slopes or sagebrush-steppe openings.

directions: A widespread Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest native of dry, rocky slopes, sagebrush steppe, and open pine woodland, forming a mounded clump of woolly gray-green leaves topped by broad, flat-topped umbels of cream to pale yellow flowers in early to midsummer that often blush rusty pink with age. It is an important nectar plant for native bees and a larval host for several blue butterflies, and its dried flower heads feed songbirds into winter. Grow in lean, sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; avoid fertile garden soil and supplemental summer water, both of which shorten its lifespan and cause weak, floppy growth. Well suited to rock gardens, dry slopes, and high-elevation xeriscape borders.

planting.note: Sow in fall for natural winter cold stratification, into lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun on open slopes or scablands.

directions: A Pacific Northwest and Intermountain West native of basalt scablands, dry bluffs, and open pine woodland, distinguished by large, arrow- or heart-shaped basal leaves that are woolly white beneath, from which naked flowering stalks rise to hold broad umbels of cream to sulfur-yellow flowers in late spring to early summer. Flowers are a magnet for native bees, butterflies, and other pollinators during a period when few other dryland natives are blooming, and the plant serves as a larval host for several blue butterfly species. Plant in lean, sharply drained rocky or sandy soil in full sun; established plants need no summer irrigation and resent rich soil or heavy mulch. A striking choice for rock gardens, dry slopes, and native pollinator borders in the interior Northwest.

planting.note: Sow in fall so seed overwinters and cold-stratifies naturally, into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun on open, rocky ground.

directions: A low, mat-forming buckwheat of dry, rocky ridges, scablands, and sagebrush openings from the Columbia Basin through the northern Rockies, with small, spoon-shaped gray-green leaves hugging the ground beneath short flowering stalks of pale yellow to cream, sometimes pink-tinged, flowers in mid to late spring. Its early bloom time makes it a critical nectar source for native bees emerging in spring, and it hosts several species of blue butterfly larvae. Grow in lean, sharply drained gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; it thrives on neglect and declines quickly in rich or regularly irrigated garden beds. Excellent as a groundcover in rock gardens, gravel gardens, and dry, sunny slopes where little else will grow.

planting.note: Sow in fall for natural cold stratification, into lean, sandy or gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun on open, dry ground.

directions: A shrubby buckwheat of arid sagebrush steppe and sandy scabland from the Columbia Basin through the Great Basin, forming a rounded clump of narrow white-woolly leaves topped from late summer into fall by dense, snowy-white flower clusters that stand out sharply against surrounding dormant grasses. Because it blooms later than most other native buckwheats, it provides an outsized late-season nectar resource for native bees, wasps, and migrating butterflies preparing for winter. Grow in lean, sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun with no summer irrigation once established; it is highly drought tolerant and poorly suited to amended or clay garden soil. A valuable addition to dryland pollinator gardens and restoration plantings where fall-blooming natives are scarce.

planting.note: Sow in fall so seed cold-stratifies naturally, into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun on dry, rocky or gravelly ground.

directions: A Great Plains and Southern Rocky Mountain native of dry limestone outcrops, shortgrass prairie, and open pinyon-juniper woodland, forming a tidy mound of felted gray-green leaves beneath wiry stems carrying rounded clusters of creamy white to pale yellow flowers from midsummer into fall. It is an outstanding, long-blooming nectar source for native bees and butterflies during the hottest, driest part of the season when few other prairie perennials are still flowering. Grow in lean, sharply drained, rocky or gravelly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is extremely drought and heat tolerant and needs no supplemental water once established, declining if planted in rich or regularly irrigated beds. A favorite of xeriscape and shortgrass prairie plantings across the High Plains and Front Range.
sources: Plant Select (Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil along streambanks or seepy rock outcrops; keep evenly moist through establishment.

directions: A high-elevation Appalachian native of rocky streambanks, wet cliff seeps, and montane riverside outcrops in Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina, producing narrow basal leaves and upright stems topped by the largest flower heads in the genus, a fluffy pink to lavender powder-puff of tubular florets in late spring to early summer. The nectar-rich blooms draw a steady stream of native bees and butterflies during an otherwise quiet early-season window for streamside pollinator plants. Grow in consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in partial sun, mimicking the splash zone of mountain streams and rock seeps it inhabits in the wild; avoid soil that dries out or stays waterlogged and stagnant. A choice, uncommon native for rain gardens, streambank plantings, and moist rock gardens in cooler climates.
